content: Sickle cell disease is a genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, characterized by abnormal hemoglobin that leads to dehydration of red blood cells and painful vaso-occlusive crises. These crises are frequent and cause significant pain, contributing to various clinical complications, increased mortality, and reduced life expectancy compared to the general population. Experimental research has indicated that intravenous magnesium is well-tolerated in hospitalized patients experiencing acute painful crises. It has shown potential to reduce the duration of hospital stays. Additionally, some in vitro studies and open-label trials of long-term oral magnesium therapy have suggested a possible benefit in pain relief, although they have not demonstrated consistent efficacy. Oral magnesium may help prevent dehydration of sickle red blood cells and reduce the recurrence of painful episodes. However, there is a need for robust evidence to evaluate the impact of both oral and intravenous magnesium on pain frequency, hospital stay duration, and quality of life. The objective of this review was to assess the effects of short-term intravenous magnesium on hospital stay duration and quality of life in children and adults with sickle cell disease. It also aimed to evaluate the impact of long-term oral magnesium therapy on the frequency of painful crises and quality of life in the same population. The review included five randomized, placebo-controlled studies involving 386 participants aged between 3 and 53 years. Two of these studies (n = 306) were short-term trials comparing intravenous magnesium sulfate to placebo (normal saline) in patients hospitalized for vaso-occlusive crises. The evidence quality for these studies was moderate, limited by risk of bias and imprecision. The intravenous magnesium doses varied between studies, with one using 100 mg/kg and the other 40 mg/kg every eight hours. One study (n = 104) reported mean daily pain scores during hospitalization, but there was no significant difference between the magnesium and placebo groups (moderate-quality evidence). Another study (n = 202) assessed quality of life scores reported by children and parents, but no differences were observed between treatment groups (low-quality evidence). Data from one study (n = 106) showed no difference in hospital stay duration between groups (low-quality evidence). Adverse events were reported in both studies but were not categorized by severity. One study noted that more participants receiving intravenous magnesium experienced warmth at the infusion site compared to placebo, but no other significant differences in adverse events were observed (low-quality evidence). Three studies (n = 80) evaluated oral magnesium pidolate compared to placebo. Two of these studies had a cross-over design, while the third was a parallel factorial study comparing hydroxyurea and oral magnesium to each other and to placebo. Only the comparison of oral magnesium to placebo was included in this review. The evidence quality for these studies was very low, with significant uncertainty in the results. None of the studies provided analyzable data on quality of life or hospital stay duration. One study (n = 24) reported no difference in the number of painful days between the magnesium and placebo groups (low-quality evidence). Two studies (n = 68) found no differences in magnesium levels in plasma or red blood cells between groups (moderate-quality evidence). Adverse events were reported in two studies (n = 56). One study noted mild diarrhea and headache, which resolved without discontinuing treatment. The other study reported gastrointestinal disorders, headache or migraine, upper respiratory infections, and rash, all of which were evenly distributed across treatment groups (moderate-quality evidence). In conclusion, the evidence, ranging from moderate to low quality, suggests that neither intravenous magnesium nor oral magnesium therapy has a significant effect on reducing painful crises, shortening hospital stays, or improving quality of life in individuals with sickle cell disease. As a result, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the clinical benefits of magnesium therapy in this context. Further randomized controlled trials, potentially involving multiple centers, are needed to determine whether intravenous or oral magnesium therapies can improve health outcomes in people with sickle cell disease.
